Years 11–13 The Arts – Performing Arts

Learning expectations
Through Performing Arts, students develop strong foundations in creative thinking, performance
practice, critical reflection, and communication of artistic ideas and intent. They are taught how to
develop, refine, analyse, and present artistic works individually and collaboratively across a wide
range of authentic contexts.

The learning area supports students to build understanding of both the core concepts and
components of creating and performing, as well as the cultural, historical, and contemporary
contexts that influence contemporary performing arts practice.


Key features of the refreshed learning area
•   Clear progression from Years | Tau 9–10 through to advanced specialist performing arts
    pathways.
•   Strong emphasis on creative development, performance practice, critical reflection, and the
    communication of meaning through artistic forms.
•   Explicit teaching of disciplinary writing, helping students to communicate, explain, and evaluate
    using appropriate performing arts terminology.
•   Greater visibility of composition, devising, choreography, production technologies, creative
    processes, and artistic decision-making.
•   Purpose-built pathways that support students | mokopuna with different interests, strengths,
    and future aspirations.
•   Strong connections between creative practice and authentic artistic contexts, including culture,
    community, industry, and technology.


Subjects
Subjects within The Arts – Performing Arts Learning Area are:

•   Years 11–13 Performing Arts – Dance
•   Years 11–13 Performing Arts – Drama
•   Years 11–13 Performing Arts – Music
•   Years 12–13 Performing Arts – Music Technology
•   Years 11–13 Te Ao Haka.

Learning and pathways

Years 11–13 Performing Arts – Dance
Students are taught dance through choreography, performance, responding to dance, and dance
making. Students are taught literacy in dance as they examine dance elements, vocabularies,
processes, principles, and technologies related to dance across diverse purposes, contexts, and
forms. Students develop an understanding of how they can use their bodies to communicate ideas
and meaning.

Strands

Years 11–13 Dance is organised into four strands:

•   Creating
•   Responding
•   Performing
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Years 11–13 Dance leads to pathways in choreography, performance, research, and related areas
such as creative arts, design, movement practices, arts administration, education, movement
therapy, and cultural, social, or historical studies.

Years 11–13 Performing Arts – Drama
Students are taught how to examine dramatic forms, conventions, and performance styles in
relation to cultural and historical contexts, and apply this knowledge in the creation and
presentation of dramatic work. They develop technical, collaborative, and interpretive skills,
alongside critical reflection and informed appreciation of artistic works.

Strands

Years 11–13 Drama is organised into four strands:

•   Process and Performance
•   Making and Creating
•   Contexts and Influences
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Years 11–13 Drama leads to pathways in drama and related disciplines, such as creative
industries, law, communication, humanities, and education.

Years 11–13 Music
Students are taught core musical concepts through creating, performing, and analysing music
across a range of styles and traditions. They are taught how to identify, organise, and develop
musical ideas using contemporary tools, refine rehearsal and performance techniques, and apply
understanding of music contexts to interpret and communicate artistic intent.

Strands

Years 11–13 Music is organised into six strands:

•   Composition, Songwriting, and Arrangement
•   Performance
•   Music Contexts
•   Music Theory
•   Music Technology
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Years 11–13 Music leads to pathways in performance, composition, musicology, music education,
and related areas such as music therapy.

Years 12–13 Music Technology
Students are taught how to create, analyse, and perform music through digital and analogue
technologies. They develop musicianship through identifying and applying core concepts and
explain production processes and techniques using industry-standard terminology. Students are
taught knowledge of studio-based production, live sound, and event management to prepare them
for participation in real music ecosystems.

Strands

Years 12–13 Music Technology is organised into six strands:

•   Fundamentals of Music
•   Making and Creating
•   Music Industry
•   Music Production
•   Live Sound and Event Technology
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Years 12–13 Music Technology leads to pathways in fields such as composition, performance,
music production, audio engineering, event technology, live sound, and media.

Years 11–13 Te Ao Haka
Students | Mokopuna are taught about the whakapapa, performance conventions, creative
processes, and contexts of Te Ao Haka. They analyse and apply performance elements to
communicate meaning, develop performance expertise, and make connections across performing
arts disciplines and indigenous performance traditions.

Strands

Years 11–13 Te Ao Haka is organised into two whenu:

•   Explore, Create, and Make | Te Tūhura me te Waihanga
•   Understand and Appreciate | Te Mōhio me te Maioha.

Pathways

Years 12–13 Te Ao Haka leads to pathways in fields such as Māori performing arts, kapa haka,
teaching and education, cultural leadership, community development, creative arts, choreography,
event and festival production, research, and wider cultural and artistic professions. It also
contributes to pathways in toi Māori, the arts, teaching, tourism, cultural leadership, and global and
national performance platforms such as Te Matatini, contributing to and strengthening Aotearoa’s
economic, cultural, and creative economy.


Connections to other learning areas
The Performing Arts connects strongly with:

•   Science through anatomy, biomechanics, environmental and sustainability considerations
•   Technology through designing, creating, and using technologies to support artistic expression
•   Social Sciences through the study of people, cultures, histories and societies
•   Health and Physical Education through body awareness, working collaboratively, leadership
    and participation
•   English through disciplinary writing, communication, storytelling, language and interpretation.


How to design a programme
•   When designing teaching programmes, teachers should have a clear overview of the full
    curriculum for their subject, including the teaching sequence and any accompanying
    specifications, and context requirements, or other curriculum requirements, at each year level.
•   Programmes should be deliberately planned to provide coverage, coherence, and progression
    within and across each year, recognising that different Performing Arts subjects have
    distinctive approaches to programme design and sequencing, which should be carefully read.
•   Teachers should use the subject-specific teaching sequence guidance to support decisions
    about how learning is organised and integrated within their programme.
